title: Stop Calling the Real API: Build and Test n8n Workflows with Message Template
text: Every n8n developer knows the loop. You are building a workflow that starts with a webhook, a SOAP service, an SFTP drop or a vendor API. To test the next node, you have to run the first one again. Every tweak means another call, another file download, another 4 MB response parsed in the editor, and sometimes another rate-limit warning or a record that was only supposed to be processed once. There is a better way to work: replace the source with a message you control . The Message Template community node does exactly that, and it turns out to be a handy development tool as well as a production one. What it does Message Template renders content from an n8n expression template and outputs it as text, JSON, XML or a file , once per item or combined across all items. You write the content in the Template field, mix in expressions like {{ $json.name }} , and pick the output format. The node parses it into real structured data, so everything downstream behaves as if it came from the real source. That is the whole trick: the node can pretend to be your source . The problem with testing against the real thing When you develop against live sources, a few things go wrong over time: Heavy payloads slow the editor. A large JSON response or XML export makes the output panel sluggish, and every re-run pays that cost again. Slow and flaky upstreams. You wait on the network for data you have already seen twenty times. Side effects and limits. Some APIs count calls against a quota, trigger notifications, or return different data on the second request. Files are awkward. Re-downloading or re-reading a file on every test run is tedious, and sensitive files should not be sitting in your workflow history at all. Edge cases are hard to get. You cannot ask a production system for “an order with a single item and an ampersand in the customer name”. The approach: a small, hand-written sample Paste a trimmed-down sample of the payload into a Message Template node, set the output format, and connect it where the real source node would go. You keep the shape of the data and drop the weight. Say your workflow normally receives a large XML order export. In development, use this instead (Output Format XML ): <orders> <order id="A1"> <customer>Ann</customer> <total currency="EUR">10.50</total> <item>Pen</item> <item>Paper</item> </order> </orders> The node parses it into the same structure the XML node would give you, with attributes under $ and text under _ , so later nodes can use {{ $json.orders.order.customer }} and {{ $json.orders.order.total._ }} right away. No file, no HTTP call, no 4 MB response. The same works for the other formats: JSON: write the response body as JSON. If it is an array, you get one item per element, just like a real list endpoint. Text: mock a plain message, a log line or an HL7 segment (it can even convert line endings to CR for HL7). File: produce a small CSV or text file as binary data, ready for nodes that expect an attachment, without ever touching the disk or an FTP server. Make the sample dynamic Because the template accepts expressions, your mock does not have to be static. Feed it a handful of input items and generate one message per item: { "orderId": {{ JSON.stringify($json.id) }}, "customer": {{ JSON.stringify($json.name) }}, "amount": {{ $json.total }}, "sentAt": {{ JSON.stringify($now.toISO()) }} } Or switch to Combine All Items mode with a header, separator and footer to assemble a single document, such as one XML file holding several orders. A few input items give you a realistic multi-record payload that you wrote yourself and fully understand. Test the ugly cases on purpose This is where a hand-written source beats a live one. You can create exactly the inputs that break workflows: A single <item> where you normally get a list. (Turn on Always Use Arrays to see the difference.) A name containing & , a quote or a line break. An empty field, a missing field, a very long string. Invalid XML or JSON, to confirm your
triage_reason: Workflow testing limitation in n8n that could be solved by a tool.

title: Selling wholesale on Shopify: how do you notice when a B2B buyer stops reordering?
text: For those selling wholesale or B2B on Shopify: how do you catch a regular buyer who has quietly stopped ordering? Shopify B2B covers companies, catalogs and payment terms, but I haven’t found anything built in that flags “this account usually orders every 3 weeks and it’s been 7”. What I mostly see is someone exporting orders now and then, sorting by last order date and emailing whoever looks late, which tends to slip on busy weeks. Disclosure: I build n8n automations for Shopify B2B, and while testing a reorder reminder two things surprised me: A fixed rule like “remind after 30 days” fits almost nobody. Buyers have very different rhythms, so using each buyer’s own typical gap between past orders worked much better. Buyers whose last order hasn’t shipped yet should be skipped. A “time to reorder?” email while they’re still waiting for the last delivery looks careless. Curious how others handle it: Do you track reorder timing per buyer, or just by a fixed number of days? Does the follow-up come from sales personally, or an automated email? Has anyone found that a pre-filled “reorder the same items” link actually gets used by B2B buyers? 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic
triage_reason: B2B merchant needs a tool to automatically flag inactive wholesale accounts.
